signals.title: Introducing GPT-6.1 Terra | OpenAI
signals.excerpt:
Introducing GPT-6.1 Terra | OpenAI
# GPT-6.1 Terra
## Delivering fast and capable computer use at scale
We’re introducing **GPT-6.1 Terra**, a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos.
Terra continues to advance the cost-intelligence frontier across our model families, providing a new balance of speed, capability, and cost. Its standard API prices are 50% lower than those of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, making it practical for developers to automate high-volume work, like reading incoming invoices and entering their details into accounting software. In ChatGPT Work and Codex, your plan goes further with GPT-6.1 Terra—the same usage allowance covers more tasks than with GPT‑5.6 Terra and substantially more than with GPT‑6.1 Sol or GPT‑6 Astra.
## From visual understanding to action
We measured GPT-6.1 Terra’s computer-use capabilities on **Agents’ Last Exam,** a benchmark of professional tasks that includes turning architectural drawings into a 3D model and reviewing an animated film shot by shot to create a time-coded log for a restoration team. At medium reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Terra scores 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra at about one-third the cost. It even performs on par with GPT-6 Astra at only one-tenth its price per token. At max effort, Terra is over three times as token efficient as Claude Opus 5.5, and one-fourth its price per token, resulting in a \~9x lower cost per task. Terra is also much quicker, completing tasks **over three times faster** than both GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.
On **MMMU-Pro**, a benchmark of visual reasoning, GPT-6.1 Terra outperforms GPT-5.6 Terra at every reasoning setting. It even nearly matches the scores of our most capable frontier model, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6.1 Sol at much lower cost.
**OSWorld 2.1** tests how well AI agents use desktop apps to complete multistep tasks, such as building a 3D model from a technical drawing. At medium reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Terra surpasses GPT-5.6 Terra’s best score at a fraction of the cost per task.
## A significant step up on factuality and coding
This year, we’ve invested heavily in reducing hallucinations and factual errors produced by our models. On our internal benchmark of error-inducing prompts, the error rate at low reasoning effort fell from 53.6% with GPT-5.6 Terra to 16.7% with GPT-6.1 Terra, a drop of nearly 37 percentage points. At maximum effort, the error rate fell by 18 percentage points to 4.3%, nearly matching the rates for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.
GPT-6.1 Terra marks a substantial improvement over GPT-5.6 Terra for software engineering. **Terminal-Bench 4.0** tests how well coding agents solve problems from the command line, such as fixing a webpage whose layout shifts as it loads. At maximum reasoning effort, GPT‑6.1 Terra solves 50.3% of tasks, more than double GPT‑5.6 Terra’s published score of 21.5%. For the most complex coding tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra remain the better choice.
**Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1** tests how well agents use code to carry out scientific research tasks, such as tracking cell divisions in a time-lapse video. At max reasoning, GPT-6.1 Terra surpasses GPT-6.1 Sol at lower cost, coming within five points of Opus 5.5 at less than one-fifth the estimated cost.
## Safety and alignment
As we make powerful AI more efficient and accessible, we continue training, testing, and refining our safeguards. GPT‑6.1 Terra meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, and maintains the protections developed for GPT‑6 Astra.
GPT-6.1 Terra brings with it the alignment improvements of the GPT-6 series. According to our evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra is more likely to stay within scope and honestly disclose limitations and potential blockers to the user compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In our prompt-injection tests, GPT-6.1 Terra also showed strong resistance to malicious instructions designed to divert it from the user’s task. More detail is available in the system card⁠(opens in a new window).
## Pricing and availability
Starting today, GPT-6.1 Terra is available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Developers can also access it through the OpenAI API as `gpt-6.1-terra`.
Standard API pricing is $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 per million cached input tokens, and $5 per million output tokens.

# NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB 

 Published: October 23, 2026

# Introducing NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB

Today, we’re excited to release Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB — our latest open small language model optimized for speed and intelligence per GB in conversational agents.

Bolt E4B builds on Gemma 4 E4B with Nemotron post-training. It combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on NVIDIA GeForce RTX, Jetson, RTX Spark and DGX Spark.

Bolt E4B offers ~40% higher average quality against our prior model on key conversational agent benchmarks and outputs up to ~80% fewer tokens vs peers.

Designed to pack conversational agent intelligence into as little as ~4GB in its target workloads, Bolt E4B enables responsive local experiences while preserving headroom for applications and other models in the same pipeline.

...

After post-training, we quantized the selected BF16 checkpoint to Q4_K_M using llama.cpp with importance-matrix (imatrix) calibration. Calibration used approximately 1M tokens of RL rollouts from the same training step as the selected checkpoint.

This release also includes a DFlash parallel drafter. It proposes all draft tokens in one forward pass, which the target verifies in parallel while preserving the target model’s output distribution. DFlash delivers up to 21% higher throughput relative to Gemma-4-E4B’s original MTP drafter.

# PyTorch opens the AI ecosystem to a new class of accelerators

IBM has made Spyre a first-class PyTorch backend, giving developers the same workflows across devices.

In October 2025, IBM and the PyTorch Foundation outlined a plan for deeper Spyre enablement in 2026: treating the accelerator as a first-class PyTorch backend and supporting multi-accelerator scheduling. The latest software ecosystem

...

Spyre is IBM’s dataflow AI accelerator, optimized for inference. It is designed for enterprise teams running AI alongside their applications and data on IBM Z, LinuxONE, and Power systems. Its reduced-precision compute is well suited to the matrix-heavy work in language generation and embedding models. Unlike a conventional GPU, which executes kernels as instruction streams across scheduled groups of threads, Spyre triggers computation as data arrives at its compute engines. PyTorch provides the common layer that allows this different architecture to participate in an ecosystem built largely around GPUs.

## Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) have transformed knowledge discovery, but their use in sensitive domains is limited by privacy concerns and risks of data leakage. Moreover, LLMs may hallucinate when queried about information outside their training data, undermining their reliability for scientific, clinical, or policy-related tasks. We present MyGPT, a fully open-source, privacy-preserving retrieval-augmented-generation (RAG) platform that uses open-source LLMs and operates locally or within secure institutional environments. MyGPT empowers users to query user-defined libraries such as biomedical literature, confidential clinical documents, and multilingual global health policies, while ensuring that sensitive data never leaves the secure environment. We introduce confidence metrics, including “relevance scores” and “hallucination index,” and provide explicit source citation from the library within a single interface to assess contextual support for generated answers. MyGPT offers a cost-effective, modular, open-source alternative to commercial LLM services and democratizes knowledge-seeking across multiple domains, including use at remote facilities without internet access.

signals.title: Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs | Scientific Reports
signals.excerpt:
Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs | Scientific Reports
* Article
* Open access
* Published: 26 October 2026
# Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs
* Enmiao Feng 1,
* Gaike Wang 2,
* Pengfei Li 1,
* Yinuo Wang ORCID: orcid.org/0009-0004-3927-0742 3 &
* …
* Shan Huang 4
## Abstract
Large language model (LLM) inference workloads are bursty, have output lengths that are unknown at arrival, expose two resource-distinct phases (prefill and decode), and serve requests carrying heterogeneous service-level objectives (SLOs) on time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT). Prevailing schedulers rely on static heuristics that cannot adapt to this uncertainty, while online reinforcement learning (RL) is unsafe and sample-inefficient in production. We present URSA, an uncertainty-aware, risk-sensitive scheduler trained *entirely offline*, without interacting with a live serving system, on scheduling transitions generated by replaying historical request traces under existing heuristic schedulers. URSA (i) predicts a calibrated *distribution* over each request’s output length and derived key–value (KV) cache footprint rather than a point estimate; (ii) encodes the joint state of the waiting queue, heterogeneous GPU instances, and KV occupancy as a request–instance heterogeneous graph processed by a graph neural network; (iii) learns a dispatch policy with conservative, distributional offline RL whose reward jointly optimizes SLO attainment, goodput, and KV-overflow risk; and (iv) reserves memory at a class-dependent high quantile of the predicted footprint to bound out-of-memory events. Across the BurstGPT, Azure LLM inference, and Alibaba GPU-cluster traces, URSA raises overall SLO attainment from \\(71.3\\%\\) (FCFS) and \\(84.1\\%\\) (learning-to-rank) to \\(90.4\\%\\), cuts P99 TTFT by up to \\(3.3\\times \\), and reduces recompute/eviction events below \\(1\\%\\), approaching an oracle that knows true lengths. We analyze limitations, robustness to prediction error, and transfer to other scheduling domains.

The Amazon Bedrock inference engine delivers the performance, security, and scale required for enterprise workloads. 

You can call GPT-6.1 Terra directly through Amazon Bedrock APIs or configure ChatGPT Work and Codex to use the model on Amazon Bedrock. Use it to draft proposals, interpret technical drawings, investigate codebases, and build agents that operate across business systems. Established AWS controls help you secure workloads, govern access, and audit model invocation activity. 

You can get started in the Amazon Bedrock console or programmatically through supported Amazon Bedrock APIs. For information about supported AWS Regions, endpoints, APIs, features, inference profiles and pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation.

signals.excerpt:
Tsinghua AI Open-Sources AKV, a Cache Engineering Server for LLM Agents on SGLang - MarkTechPost

# Tsinghua AI Open-Sources AKV, a Cache Engineering Server for LLM Agents on SGLang

By

Asif Razzaq

October 26, 2026

Tsinghua University and CUHK researchers open-sourced AKV, a serving system for KV cache engineering in LLM agents. Instead of summarizing old history, agents drop selected KV cache entries and keep reusing the rest. Across 3 models and 4 agent benchmarks, average cost falls 27.7%. Average task score rises 1.7 points. The code is Apache-2.0 licensed and builds on SGLang.

...

## What does the AKV API look like?

The interface is stateless and OpenAI-compatible. Clients send the full message history and two optional fields. `drop_message` maps a trigger message index to the messages to drop. `reposition` lists the indices after which positions get compacted.

A `CachePolicy` builds those fields from a trigger, a selector and a reposition rule. Built-in policies are turn-based, token-based or model-based. A `CacheTool` lets the model call `drop_context` itself.

signals.title: FP4 W/A+FP4 KV的强化学习也能「又快又稳」：阿里千问提出TRACE，Rollout最高加速5.4倍
signals.excerpt:
FP4 W/A+FP4 KV的强化学习也能「又快又稳」：阿里千问提出TRACE，Rollout最高加速5.4倍 

 FP4 W/A+FP4 KV的强化学习也能「又快又稳」：阿里千问提出TRACE，Rollout最高加速5.4倍 

 AI技术研报 2026-10-24 13:41 +5940 阅读

大模型强化学习越来越「吃算力」，最昂贵的环节之一正是 Rollout。把 Rollout 从 BF16 压到 FP4，理论上可以显著降低计算和显存开销，但问题也随之而来 —— 训练端与 Rollout 端即使面对非常接近的数值，也可能因为 FP4 的离散量化边界而落到不同码点，最终把微小的数值误差放大成策略偏差导致训练崩溃。

阿里千问联合俄亥俄州立大学的研究团队提出了 TRACE。它的核心思路并不是继续分别提高训练端和 Rollout 端的量化精度，而是直接减少两条低精度执行路径之间的差异：用 Rollout 侧真实的 FP4 量化结果，反过来指导训练侧的舍入方向。在 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B、Qwen3.5-122B-A10B、Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 以及 Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B 四个 MoE 模型上，TRACE 可以在联合 FP4 W/A 与 FP4 KV Cache Rollout 的设置下，将最终性能拉回到 BF16 Rollout 附近，同时在 128K 输出长度下 rollout 获得最高 5.4× 的解码吞吐提升。

- 论文标题：TRACE: Rollout-Guided Quantization-Aware Training for FP4 Reinforcement Learning of MoE Language Models
- ArXiv 链接：https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07767
- Huggingface 链接：https://huggingface.co/papers/2610.07767

...

TRACE 的第一个设计是 Rollout-Guided Quantization-Aware Training。在 Rollout 阶段，系统记录 FP4 routed expert 激活和 FP4 KV 状态对应的量化结果；到了后续训练阶段，这些信息不再只是「历史数据」，而是直接参与训练侧 fake quantization 的舍入决策。具体来说，对于训练侧某个待量化值，TRACE 仍然只在相邻的两个 FP4 E2M1 码点之间选择，但不再机械使用标准 round-to-nearest （RTN）。它会优先选择距离 Rollout 侧实际码点更近的那个候选值。

图 3：TRACE 总体流程。Rollout 侧保存紧凑量化信息，训练侧加载后用于调整 FP4 舍入。

然而，直接保存完整的 Rollout 量化结果并不便宜。这些信息需要经历 GPU→CPU、CPU 缓存、磁盘写入 / 读取，再在训练时回到 GPU；长轨迹、大 batch 和异步 RL 都会放大存储与通信压力。 TRACE 的第二个设计，正是把「需要传什么」压到最少。作者统计发现，超过 99% 的训练 /rollout 量化不一致只相差一个相邻 FP4 codebook entry。既然训练侧自身的激活值已经把候选范围压得很小，那么 Rollout 侧没必要把完整低精度值全部传过去；保留少量 mantissa 信息，加上 scale，通常就足够告诉训练侧应该朝哪个方向舍入。

...

实验效果

在 Qwen3.5-35B-A3B 的 RL 任务上，TRACE 的平均分达到 75.3。作为对照，BF16 Rollout 为 74.9，普通 QAT 为 59.6，QaRL 为 58.6，QUADS 为 68.8。尤其在 HMMT25 上，TRACE 从 QUADS 的 59.0 提升到 70.0。

论文专门测了 Rollout 吞吐和端到端 RL step time。结果显示，如果保存完整指导信息，通信开销确实会严重拖慢 Rollout；而采用紧凑缓存后，TRACE 的吞吐基本贴近原生 FP4 Rollout。在 8K 输入、128K 输出时，解码吞吐相对 BF16 Rollout 最高提升 5.4×。端到端来看，联合 FP4 Rollout 的 RL step time 中 TRACE 仅产生约 7.4% 的额外开销。

# PyTorch Conference 2026: Google and Meta Open-Source TorchTPU for Native PyTorch on TPUs 

Oct 25, 2026 4 min read 

by

- Andrew Hoblitzell 

At PyTorch Conference North America 2026 in San Jose, Google and Meta open-sourced TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend for Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). Meta, which created PyTorch in 2016, plans to move larger-scale LLM workloads onto TPUs with it, Meta software engineer Zongwei Zhou said in the October 21 keynotes.

TorchTPU replaces PyTorch/XLA, a lazy-tensor bridge from 2020 that, according to the announcement, "required intrusive source-code modifications." The new backend aims to make porting a model as simple as changing `model.to("cuda")` to `model.to("tpu")`. "With TorchTPU, TPUs join GPUs and CPUs as a native option for PyTorch," Google Cloud wrote in its announcement, co-authored by Bill Jia, VP of engineering for Core ML/AI.

...

Because TorchTPU plugs into PyTorch's low-level dispatcher, the speakers said, Hugging Face models worked with it out of the box. The vLLM and SGLang inference engines run natively, and TorchTitan supports dense, mixture-of-experts, and diffusion models for training at scale. Ray and llm-d scale TPU workloads across hosts on Kubernetes. Four repositories were open sourced: TorchTPU, vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, and TorchTitan.

Jia showed near-linear scaling past 8,000 TPU chips, with per-chip throughput holding roughly constant as the cluster grew. Google's published results include a Qwen3 235B mixture-of-experts run on 8,192 TPU v7x chips at 28% model FLOPs utilization. The announcement is candid that the one-line change is only a starting point:

> One cannot achieve peak TPU performance with that simple change, since a model's shapes, sharding and ops may be skewed toward a GPU architecture; however, the model should run out of the box.

Hugging Face has released 207 versioned WebGPU kernels, a JavaScript loader and Fleet benchmarking for local browser AI workloads.

Published

On this page More than a folder of shaders

Hugging Face has released (opens in a new tab) an initial collection of 207 open-source WebGPU kernels for local AI workloads, accompanied by a JavaScript library that downloads and runs them directly from the Hugging Face Hub. Announced by Nico Martin (opens in a new tab) and Joshua Lochner (opens in a new tab), the collection covers the low-level operations that browser inference runtimes repeatedly need: matrix multiplication, normalization, convolution, attention primitives, quantization, broadcasting and tensor layout transformations. Everything is Apache 2.0 licensed. This is foundational work rather than another model demo. Faster browser inference ultimately depends on faster individual operations, and WebGPU portability alone does not guarantee good performance across every device.

...

## Faster on an Apple M4, with caveats

Hugging Face compared its kernels against ORT WebGPU on an Apple M4 GPU using a development version of ONNX Runtime Web 1.30.0. The evaluation started with 1,756 cases across all 207 operations. Hugging Face’s published aggregate covers the 809 cases where both systems produced matching outputs and reliable timings. Familiar operations showed more moderate improvements: Add reached 3.52x, Softmax 2.11x, LayerNormalization 2.22x and MatMul 1.14x. Some specialized workloads produced extreme results. signals.title: AMD Adds MiniMax-M3.1 Support for Instinct MI350 Series GPUs | TokenPost
signals.excerpt:
# AMD Adds MiniMax-M3.1 Support for Instinct MI350 Series GPUs

The ROCm update supports vLLM and ATOM. AMD measured lower decode latency and higher interactivity in selected tests.

By Simon Yoon

Published Oct 23, 2026, 5:57 PM EDT

A black accelerator module rests on a vivid red platform / TokenPost.ai

AMD announced Thursday, Oct. 22, that MiniMax-M3.1 can run on Instinct MI350 Series GPUs through ROCm versions of vLLM and ATOM, bringing a coding and agent model with a context window of one million tokens to AMD’s inference stack.

MiniMax-M3.1 includes reasoning and tool-use features. AMD’s setup supports the original NVFP4 checkpoint after conversion during loading, as well as an MXFP4 export made with AMD Quark. The ATOM configuration AMD tested uses the Quark export. AITER kernels handle expert routing, attention and reduction operations. AMD said the two weight paths performed within evaluation error of each other on GSM8K, AIME and MMMU-Pro.

ATOM applies per-channel FP8 attention and combines shared-expert work during startup. It also uses CUDA graphs to capture DSpark’s draft pass; AMD’s tests found that roughly half of DSpark’s seven-token draft proposals were accepted on real text. The MI350 implementation uses four-way tensor parallelism per replica, allowing two replicas on an eight-GPU node.

In AMD’s tests, vLLM mono decode reduced per-token decode latency by a factor of 3.2 at one request, 2.1 at four and 1.5 at 16, compared with the same server with mono decode disabled. On coding-agent traces, AMD said mono decode produced 2.2x to 2.4x the interactivity across one to eight concurrent users. Pairing it with DSpark speculative decoding increased interactivity by about one-third for one to four users and 13% at eight users in the reported tests.

The current configuration supports mono decode with DSpark for up to four concurrent requests. Wider decode steps use the standard path. AMD listed wider mono-decode steps and support for MiniMax-M3.1 mono decode in ATOM as future work, without a timeline.

In a separate announcement on Oct. 12, AMD introduced its Helion rack-scale design for agentic AI workloads; its enterprise configuration supports up to 16 Instinct MI350P GPUs.

signals.title: Google ML Drift Accelerates On-Device AI Inference Across Diverse GPUs - InfoQ
signals.excerpt:
Google has released ML Drift, an open-source, cross-platform GPU compute engine designed for on-device AI and machine learning inference. Licensed under Apache 2.0, it abstracts the complexities of different GPU hardware and low-level APIs, supporting OpenGL ES, OpenCL, Metal, and WebGPU.

ML Drift is the core GPU acceleration engine that powers LiteRT. By open-sourcing it, Google is enabling developers to build custom graphics and inference runtimes for applications ranging from traditional computer vision, audio, and depth processing to generative AI.

One of ML Drift's main goal is simplifying access to the diverse GPU hardware that developers encounter when creating applications for edge devices.

...

To achieve this, ML Drift introduces several technical improvements over the legacy TFLite GPU delegate, including unified shaders through tensor virtualization, extensible custom operations, and five-dimensional tensor support. It also incorporates hardware-specific optimizations for GPUs from Arm, Intel, and Qualcomm Technologies to "maximize hardware utilization across modern GPUs".

ML Drift extends desktop support for inference on Windows and Linux through Dawn, Chromium's WebGPU implementation, while retaining native Metal backend support on macOS. Dawn provides a unified API model leveraging WebGPU's hardware abstraction layer, avoiding the need to interface directly with platform-specific graphics APIs such as DirectX and Vulkan.

...

With the release of ML Drift, Google will stop updating the legacy TensorFlow Lite GPU delegate. For backward compatibility with existing models, the company recommends migrating to the LiteRT ML Drift GPU accelerator. Application developers can use the LiteRT ML Drift accelerator, while GPU and system engineers can access its lower level C++ API to construct custom `GpuModel` compute graphs and write custom shaders.

signals.excerpt:
# Vera Rubin Inference Results Leave Nvidia’s 75% Training Claim Untested

At about 190 output tokens per second per user, Vera Rubin reached 5.7 times GB300’s total throughput per megawatt of GPU and memory power, using a four-GPU GB300 comparison.

By Simon Yoon

Published Oct 26, 2026, 6:51 AM EDT

A calibrated power analyzer stands beside a compute rack / TokenPost.ai

Oct. 15 AA-AgentPerf results put Vera Rubin NVL72 at 5.7 times GB300’s total throughput per megawatt at a specific speed, while leaving Nvidia’s separate training estimate untested. The finding measures inference — generating outputs from a trained model — rather than a completed training run.

The benchmark exercised coding-agent tasks with DeepSeek V4 Pro. At the selected operating point, Vera Rubin produced about 190 output tokens per second for each user. GB300 rack configurations did not reach that rate, so the comparison used a four-GPU GB300 setup. The 5.7-times result reflects that configuration and speed, rather than a full-rack comparison.

The power measure includes the GPUs and their memory but excludes CPUs, networking and cooling. The per-user speed leaves out time to first token, or the interval before a model begins responding. The total-throughput calculation also includes cached input tokens. When the systems were measured at their respective throughput peaks, Vera Rubin’s total throughput per megawatt was 1.14 times GB300’s.

## Abacus brings its Nemotron fine-tune down to four bits

Abacus.AI published Smaug-Nemotron-3.5-NVFP4 on October 22, a four-bit version of its agentic coding fine-tune of NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. The base model has 120 billion parameters, with 12 billion active at a time; it combines Mamba-2, mixture-of-experts layers and attention, and accepts text, images and video. Abacus says the new checkpoint occupies about 75 GB, roughly a third of the BF16 model’s size.

That smaller footprint changes the hardware needed to serve the model. Abacus’s post describes NVIDIA’s corresponding NVFP4 checkpoint as running on one DGX Spark, one H200 or one GB200. It also says existing stacks serving that checkpoint can use Smaug as a drop-in replacement. The weights are published on Hugging Face under the OpenMDW 1.1 license inherited from NVIDIA’s base model.

...

## Training against the weights that will ship

Abacus says ordinary fine-tuning followed by four-bit quantization would erase much of the small update it wanted to preserve. Its approach, which it calls merge-aware training, runs each training step using weights rounded into the format intended for release. The learning objective rewards tool-call actions while applying a separate penalty to keep the model’s reasoning close to the base.

> “The new idea here is that the loss always sees the model exactly as it will be served.”
> 
> Sandeep Singh Sandha and Arvind Sundararajan, the authors, write

The method adapts the language model, according to the company; the vision encoder, vision-language connector, MTP head and quantization layout remain those of NVIDIA’s checkpoint. That leaves the fine-tune’s main change in how the model behaves during multi-turn tool use, not in its architecture.

signals.title: Cerebras trillion-parameter model deployment — Grafy News
signals.excerpt:
read

Cerebras has published a detailed account of how it runs multi-trillion-parameter models across dozens of wafer-scale processors, describing a pipeline in which model weights stay on chip and only activations travel between wafers at roughly two microseconds per hop. It matters because the post turns an abstract claim about frontier-scale inference into a specific architecture, with trade-offs developers can inspect and test.

...

A single WSE-3T wafer provides 44 GB of on-chip memory, according to Cerebras, while trillion-parameter models need terabytes for their weights alone. The answer is to spread the model across many wafers rather than squeeze it into one.

The worked example is Kimi K3, described as an open-source model with about 3 trillion parameters, 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers. Cerebras assumes 4-bit weight quantization, in the manner of the Hugging Face implementation, an 8-bit KV cache, and a 256k assumed average request size.

On those assumptions, each of the model's 93 layers comes to roughly 16 GB. Because a layer fits comfortably inside 44 GB, Cerebras can keep whole layers resident on a chip instead of splitting them across wafers.

...

Cerebras executes models as a pipeline. Its compiler maps model layers across regions of wafers, and the runtime maps the path tokens travel between them. Only activations cross between wafers, over RDMA over Ethernet, at roughly two microseconds per hop; weights generally do not move at all.

The assembly-line analogy in the post: wafer 1 runs layers 1–2 and sends activations to wafer 2, which runs layers 3–4 and passes results to wafer 3, until the last wafer produces the next token. Cerebras says production deployments use much finer-grained stages than the illustration.

...

The example is not a toy model. As described in Cerebras's post, Kimi K3 scores 88.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, against 88.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol, and 91.2% on BrowseComp, against 90.4% for GPT-5.6 Sol. Open-weight models in the multi-trillion-parameter class are becoming servable at high token rates, and the architecture described here is a plausible reason why.

The caveat matters just as much. Cerebras notes that performance comparisons rest on third-party benchmarking or internal testing, and that observed speed improvements versus GPU-based systems may vary with workload, configuration, date and models tested.
